hints: Start by drawing out $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CHCH(OH)CH}_3$ and look for two different features, a C=C double bond and a carbon with four different groups.
The C2=C3 double bond can exist as E and Z forms, which already gives you 2 geometric stereoisomers.
Now check C4 with its OH group for chirality and multiply the independent E/Z possibilities by the independent R/S possibilities to get the total.
walkthrough:
**Draw the structure**

Think of this like a detective, first sketch what you have. Pent-2-en-4-ol is $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}=\text{CH}-\text{CH(OH)}-\text{CH}_3$.

Structure:
$$\text{C1H}_3-\text{C2H}=\text{C3H}-\text{C4H(OH)}-\text{C5H}_3$$

**Spot the E/Z isomerism**

A C=C bond cannot rotate, so different groups can be locked on the same side or opposite sides. At C2=C3, each carbon has H and a carbon chain, so both E (opposite) and Z (same side) forms exist.

Count so far:
$$2 \text{ geometric isomers (E and Z)}$$

**Spot the optical isomerism**

Now look at C4. It is bonded to H, OH, $\text{CH}_3$, and $\text{CH=CHCH}_3$. That is four different groups, so C4 is a chiral centre.

Count for this centre:
$$2 \text{ optical isomers (R and S)}$$

**Combine independent types**

E/Z and R/S are independent of each other, so every E/Z form can pair with every R/S form. Just multiply them.

Total:
$$2 \times 2 = 4 \text{ stereoisomers}$$

options.A: 2 counts only one type of stereoisomerism. You get 2 if you count only E and Z, or only the two enantiomers at C4, but this molecule shows both types at the same time.
options.B: 3 is a common miscount when students add 2 + 1 or think one form is meso. There is no plane of symmetry here, so no meso form is lost, and independent stereoelements multiply, they do not add.
options.C: 4 is correct because 2 E/Z forms at the C2=C3 double bond multiplied by 2 optical forms at the chiral C4 centre gives 4 distinct stereoisomers.
options.D: 5 is too high. There is only one C=C bond giving E/Z and only one chiral centre giving a pair of enantiomers. No extra stereocentre or double bond exists to make a fifth isomer.
